cards.q: What is client-server architecture?
cards.a: A **client** asks for something. A **server** does the work and sends back an answer. Almost every app works like this.

cards.q: What can be a client?
cards.a: The thing the user uses, like a web browser or a mobile app. It can also be **another server**: when your server asks a payment company to charge a card, your server is the client.

cards.q: Why not do everything on the client?
cards.a: **Shared data:** everyone sees the same data, kept in one place. **Safety:** you can't trust the client. **Power:** a server can be a big, fast machine; a phone has a small battery and little memory.

cards.q: Why must important checks, like the price, happen on the server?
cards.a: **Never trust the client.** Anyone can change the app on their own phone or browser, like changing a price from 1,000 to 1. If the check happens on the server, this trick does not work.

cards.q: What should you draw first in almost every design?
cards.a: **Client → Server → Database**. Draw this first, then improve it. And say out loud that all important checks happen on the server.

cards.q: What is a packet?
cards.a: A small piece of data. Data is not sent as one big piece: it is cut into packets. A 1 MB photo becomes about 700 packets of about 1,500 bytes each.

cards.q: What can go wrong with packets on the way, and what fixes it?
cards.a: Packets of the same photo can take different roads, arrive **out of order**, or get **lost**. **TCP** puts them back in order and asks again for the lost ones.

cards.q: Latency vs bandwidth: what is the difference?
cards.a: **Latency** = how long one trip takes. **Bandwidth** = how much data can travel at the same time. More bandwidth doesn't lower latency, just as more lanes don't make a trip shorter.

cards.q: When does latency matter most, and when does bandwidth?
cards.a: **Latency** matters most for a web page with many small requests. **Bandwidth** matters most for a big download, like a movie.

cards.q: About how long is a round trip over different distances?
cards.a: Inside one data center: 0.5 ms. Same city: 5 ms. US East Coast ↔ Europe: 80 ms. India ↔ USA: 200 ms.

cards.q: Why do big apps run servers in many countries and use a CDN?
cards.a: **Distance adds delay.** If users are in India and servers are in the USA, every single request waits about 200 ms just for travel. Keeping data close to users makes the trip short.

cards.q: What is an IP address, and what is a port?
cards.a: An **IP address** tells you which computer, like a building's address. A **port** tells you which app on that computer, like the flat number inside the building.

cards.q: IPv4 vs IPv6: what is the difference?
cards.a: **IPv4** looks like `192.168.1.10` and has only about 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough. **IPv6** looks like `2001:db8::1`: longer, with a huge number of addresses. It is slowly replacing IPv4.

cards.q: Public IP vs private IP: what is the difference?
cards.a: A **public IP** can be reached from anywhere on the internet, like a building's street address. A **private IP** only works inside one network, like room numbers inside an office.

cards.q: What is NAT?
cards.a: **Network Address Translation.** Your home router has one public IP and gives each device a private IP. When a device talks to the internet, the router swaps its private address for the public one.

cards.q: Why should only the load balancer have a public IP?
cards.a: App servers and databases stay on private IPs inside the data center, so nobody on the internet can reach your database directly. This is much safer.

cards.q: Which port numbers should you know?
cards.a: Ports go from 0 to 65535. Know **80** HTTP, **443** HTTPS, **22** SSH, **5432** PostgreSQL, **3306** MySQL, **6379** Redis and **27017** MongoDB.

cards.q: What is DNS?
cards.a: The **Domain Name System**. It turns a **name** like `google.com` into an **IP address**. It is the contact list of the internet.

cards.q: In what order does a computer look up a website name?
cards.a: Browser cache → computer (OS) cache → DNS resolver → root server → .com server → the domain's name server. From fastest to slowest.

cards.q: Long TTL vs short TTL: what is the tradeoff?
cards.a: **Long** (like 1 day): fewer lookups, but after an IP change some users go to the old one for up to a day. **Short** (like 1 minute): changes reach everyone quickly, but more lookups.

cards.q: What do the DNS records A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and NS do?
cards.a: **A:** name → IPv4. **AAAA:** name → IPv6. **CNAME:** name → another name (an alias). **MX:** where to send email for the domain. **NS:** which name servers are in charge of the domain.

cards.q: What is GeoDNS?
cards.a: DNS that gives a different answer depending on where the user is, so each user goes to the nearest region. Inside each region, a load balancer spreads the traffic across servers.

cards.q: Why is DNS not enough for load balancing on its own?
cards.a: DNS can return several IPs for one name, and each client picks one. It is simple, but slow to react when a server dies, because the old answers stay cached. So we put a real load balancer behind DNS.

cards.q: TCP vs UDP: what is the basic difference?
cards.a: **TCP** is like a tracked courier: safe and in order, but a little slower. **UDP** is like throwing flyers from a moving car: very fast, but nobody checks if each one arrived.

cards.q: How does the TCP handshake work?
cards.a: Three short messages open the connection before any data moves: **SYN** (can we talk?), **SYN-ACK** (yes, can you hear me?), **ACK** (yes!).

cards.q: Why do apps reuse open TCP connections?
cards.a: The handshake costs **one full round trip** before any data is sent. From India to a server in the USA, that is about 200 ms of waiting.

cards.q: When should you pick UDP instead of TCP?
cards.a: **Use TCP by default.** Pick UDP only when old data is useless: voice and video calls, and online games, where a late update is worse than a missing one.

cards.q: Why is streaming video, even a live stream, not a UDP case?
cards.a: The video is sent as small chunks over normal HTTP, through a CDN. The player keeps a few seconds of video ready, so a resent packet is never noticed.

cards.q: What is QUIC?
cards.a: A protocol Google created. It runs on **UDP** and adds TCP's safety on top, but sets up connections faster and works better on phones. **HTTP/3** uses QUIC.

cards.q: What does it mean that HTTP is stateless?
cards.a: The server forgets you after every request. That is why the browser sends a **cookie** or a **token** with every single request.

cards.q: What three things does TLS give you?
cards.a: **Privacy:** nobody can read the data. **No tampering:** nobody can change it on the way. **The right server:** you are really talking to `bank.com`, checked with a certificate.

cards.q: Why does a new HTTPS connection wait about two round trips?
cards.a: One round trip for the TCP handshake, plus one more for the TLS handshake, before any data moves. Another reason to **reuse connections**.

cards.q: What is TLS termination?
cards.a: HTTPS ends at the **load balancer**. It decrypts the request and passes it to the app servers over the private network. Many companies now encrypt the inside traffic too, especially for sensitive data (**zero trust**).

cards.q: Why end TLS at the load balancer?
cards.a: Certificates live in one place, app servers don't spend CPU on encryption, and the load balancer can read the request to send `/api` and `/images` to different servers.

cards.q: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: what changed?
cards.a: **HTTP/1.1:** one request at a time on each connection. **HTTP/2:** many requests at the same time on one connection. **HTTP/3:** runs on QUIC (UDP), so one lost packet doesn't make everything else wait.

cards.q: What do "safe" and "idempotent" mean for an HTTP method?
cards.a: **Safe:** it changes nothing. **Idempotent:** doing it once or many times gives the same result.

cards.q: Which HTTP methods are safe, and which are idempotent?
cards.a: Of the five main methods, only `GET` is safe (`HEAD` and `OPTIONS` are safe too). `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent. `PATCH` is not always idempotent, and `POST` is not.

cards.q: How does an idempotency key make a retry safe?
cards.a: The app sends a unique key, like `Idempotency-Key: 7f3a9c`. The server remembers it. If the same key comes again, it sends back the first result instead of creating a new order.

cards.q: `401` vs `403`: what is the difference?
cards.a: `401` Unauthorized: you are not logged in ("Who are you?"). `403` Forbidden: you are logged in, but not allowed ("I know who you are, but no").

cards.q: When should a client retry a failed request?
cards.a: On `5xx`, `429` or no answer, but only if the request is safe to repeat: `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, or a `POST` with an idempotency key. Don't retry other `4xx`: fix the request first.

cards.q: How long should a client wait before it retries?
cards.a: Wait longer each time (**backoff**), plus a little random extra time (**jitter**), so thousands of clients don't all retry at the same moment. If the server sends `Retry-After`, wait that long.

cards.q: What are the three rules of REST?
cards.a: Everything is a **resource** (a thing, like an order). Each resource has its own **URL**, like `/orders/42`. **HTTP methods** say what you want to do with it.

cards.q: Why should REST URLs use nouns, not verbs?
cards.a: The HTTP method is already the verb. Use `POST /orders`, not `POST /createOrder`, and `DELETE /orders/42`, not `POST /orders/42/delete`.

cards.q: When should you nest REST URLs?
cards.a: Only for "belongs to": `/restaurants/17/menu-items` means the menu items of restaurant 17. Don't go deeper than one or two levels.

cards.q: How should a REST API return an error?
cards.a: With a real error code **and** a clear error body, like `409` with an `error` code and a `message`. The `error` code is for programs. The `message` is for people.

cards.q: Why take the user from the login token, never from the request body?
cards.a: Otherwise anyone could place orders as someone else.

cards.q: What should a REST API do with big lists and with changes?
cards.a: Send big lists in **pages**. Give the API a new **version** when it changes, so old apps don't break.

cards.q: How does gRPC work?
cards.a: You write a contract in a `.proto` file. A tool generates code from it for many languages. Data travels as **Protocol Buffers**, and it runs on **HTTP/2**, so many calls share one connection.

cards.q: What are the good and bad sides of gRPC?
cards.a: **Good:** very fast, and both sides must follow the same contract, so mistakes show up early. **Bad:** browsers can't call it directly (you need **gRPC-Web**, usually with a proxy like Envoy in between), and binary data is hard to read when you debug.

cards.q: What is GraphQL?
cards.a: A way for the client to ask for **exactly the data it needs** in one query, and get it back in exactly that shape.

cards.q: What are over-fetching and under-fetching?
cards.a: **Over-fetching:** getting more than you need, like 30 fields when you need only the name. **Under-fetching:** one request is not enough, so you need many round trips.

cards.q: What are the downsides of GraphQL?
cards.a: **Caching is harder**, because every request is a `POST` to the same URL. A client can send a **very expensive query**, so you need limits on depth and cost. And resolvers can cause the N+1 problem.

cards.q: When do you pick REST, gRPC or GraphQL?
cards.a: **REST** by default. **gRPC** for busy service-to-service calls inside your system. **GraphQL** when many different clients and screens need different shapes of data.

cards.q: What is wrong with polling?
cards.a: Most answers are "no", so most requests are wasted, and news can be late by up to the polling gap. 1 million users polling every 5 seconds is **200,000 requests per second**.

cards.q: What is long polling?
cards.a: The client asks, and the server **holds the request open** until there is news, or until a timeout (like 30 seconds). Then the client asks again right away.

cards.q: What is SSE (Server-Sent Events)?
cards.a: One HTTP connection that stays open, and the server sends events down it whenever it wants. Data flows **one way only**: server to client. Browsers reconnect by themselves if it drops.

cards.q: What are WebSockets good for?
cards.a: Truly real-time messages in **both directions**, with very little extra data per message: chat, games and editing together. Slack keeps a WebSocket open, so new messages arrive instantly.

cards.q: How do you choose between polling, SSE and WebSockets?
cards.a: A few seconds of delay is okay: **polling**. Mostly the server sends: **SSE**. Both sides talk: **WebSockets**. Pick the simplest option that is fast enough.

cards.q: How does a chat message reach a user connected to a different chat server?
cards.a: With **pub/sub**, like Redis Pub/Sub. Server 1 publishes the message on Ben's channel. Server 2, which holds Ben's connection, is subscribed to it, gets the message, and pushes it down Ben's WebSocket.

cards.q: How does a login session work?
cards.a: The server creates a session record (like session `abc123` = user 7) and stores it in a session store, usually Redis. You get only the session ID, in a cookie. On every request, the server looks up that ID.

cards.q: What are the good and bad sides of sessions?
cards.a: **Good:** logging out is easy. Delete the session, and the user is logged out at once, on every server (delete all their sessions to log out every device). **Bad:** every request needs a lookup in the session store.

cards.q: How does a server check a JWT?
cards.a: It checks the **signature** and the expiry time (`exp`), with **no database lookup**. If anyone changes even one letter of the payload, the signature stops matching, and the token is rejected.

cards.q: Why must you never put secrets in a JWT?
cards.a: A JWT is **signed, not encrypted**. Anyone can read the payload.

cards.q: What is the big problem with JWTs, and the usual fix?
cards.a: You can't easily take one back: it stays valid until it expires. The fix is a short-lived **access token** (like 15 minutes) plus a longer-lived **refresh token**.

cards.q: Sessions vs JWT: when do you use which?
cards.a: A normal website with one backend: **sessions in a cookie**. Many services, mobile apps or "log in with" flows: **short JWTs + refresh tokens**.

cards.q: What is a proxy?
cards.a: A server that sits **in the middle** and passes messages on someone else's behalf.

cards.q: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy: who does each one work for?
cards.a: A **forward proxy** works for the **clients**, like an office receptionist making outside calls. A **reverse proxy** works for the **servers**, like a hotel front desk.

cards.q: What is a forward proxy used for?
cards.a: Company rules (block and log websites), privacy (websites see the proxy's IP, not yours), shared caching (fetch a file once for many people), and getting around blocks in your region.

cards.q: What jobs does a reverse proxy do?
cards.a: Load balancing, HTTPS (it holds the certificate), caching, compression, security (it hides the real servers and blocks bad traffic), and routing.

cards.q: Reverse proxy vs load balancer vs API gateway: how do they relate?
cards.a: A **reverse proxy** is the general idea: a middleman for servers. A **load balancer** is one whose main job is spreading traffic. An **API gateway** adds API features: login checks, rate limits, API keys.

cards.q: What are the main steps when you type a URL and press Enter?
cards.a: Read the URL and check the browser cache → **DNS** finds the IP → **TCP** handshake → **TLS** handshake → **HTTP request** with the cookie → CDN / load balancer → app server → cache / database → **response** → the browser builds the page, with more requests for CSS, JS and images.

cards.q: About how long before the first byte, for a new HTTPS connection from India to a server in the USA?
cards.a: Three round trips of about 200 ms: the TCP handshake, the TLS 1.3 handshake, then request + response. So about **600 ms plus server time**, and more if DNS was not cached. Most of the wait is travel, not the server.

cards.q: How does a nearby CDN edge server cut the wait for a user in India?
cards.a: The handshakes become short trips, about 10 ms each. If the edge has a copy, it all takes about 30 ms. If not, the edge reuses its open connection to the origin, so only **one** long trip is left: about 280 ms instead of 650 ms.

cards.q: After the HTML arrives, how does the browser load the rest of the page?
cards.a: It finds links to CSS, JavaScript and images, and asks for them on the **connection that is already open**, many at once with HTTP/2. Then it draws the page, and the JavaScript calls APIs, like `GET /api/cart`, to fill in personal data.

cards.q: How should you answer "What happens when you type a URL?" in an interview?
cards.a: Go through **every step briefly, in order**: cache, DNS, TCP, TLS, request, servers, response, page. Give the round-trip numbers. Then ask the interviewer which part to go deeper on.
